description: We are a team that loves problem-solving and has a strong interest in everything related to technology—software, hardware, the maker world, 3D printing, and so on.
summary: Our project, MoonSite, responds to the Space Apps Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge with a web platform where lunar landing missions can be simulated from liftoff to touchdown, and replanned as situations arise that affect their course, such as a launch delay, a change of site, or the loss of light at the planned site. At every moment it recalculates the viable sites and dates from the ephemerides of the Sun and Earth, the real terrain relief, the visible fraction of the solar disk, and the windows of direct visibility to Earth, helping to make the best decision quickly and effectively.
details:
HOW DOES IT WORK?

The user chooses a landing site and a launch date. MoonSite calculates the complete mission and shows it in a single 3D scene with three scales: the Earth–Moon journey, the lunar globe, and the view standing at the site.

 

· Flight: countdown and liftoff with stage separation, parking orbit, translunar injection, coast, and lunar orbit insertion. The descent follows a real profile, and the landing is viewed from a camera on the ground.

· On the surface: the Sun and Earth are drawn over the real terrain horizon. The tool shows how long until nightfall or until the link is lost, the Sun’s elevation, the operating windows with exact times in UTC, and the estimated energy of a solar panel.

· Verdict: a color and a sentence based on editable requirements, which are the days of stay, maximum hours without sunlight, and minimum percentage of link with Earth.

· Replanning: “Simulate delay” pushes the launch back 3 days and the route is recalculated before the user’s eyes; the previous route remains as a ghost line for comparison. If the new plan fails, numbered alternatives appear that can be applied with one click.

· Comparison: up to four site and date combinations side by side, and a site-by-date grid with the verdict for each cell.

· Report: mission PDF and CSV, and direct links to NASA Moon Trek, LROC QuickMap, and JPL Horizons for the same site.

 

WHAT DOES MOONSITE OFFER?

When the schedule changes, it shows in seconds how much energy and how much link time are lost, and proposes the next window or a nearby site with more margin. With “Simulate delay” the user experiences that delay, and MoonSite offers viable alternatives, such as landing later or choosing another site on the same date. Its value lies in quantifying the light and communication margin of each site and date, in order to choose with margin and react in time when the plan changes.

 

WHAT ARE ITS ADVANTAGES?

You can run simulations of lunar landing missions, test different situations, and see the result in seconds. This translates into faster and safer decisions, and offers a unique opportunity to understand how a Moon landing is planned with real data.

 

MoonSite transforms lunar landing planning into an immersive experience:

 

· Fast, visual, and interactive.

· Accurate and based on real NASA data, with validated accuracy.

· Adaptable, replanning on the spot when something unexpected comes up.

· Accessible, with no need for specialized software; it works in the browser, on mobile too.

· Educational, helping people understand how lunar landing missions are planned and what factors can affect their course.

 

 

WHAT IS THE EXPECTED IMPACT OF THE PROJECT?

MoonSite reduces the risk of losing a mission because of a poor choice of landing site or date, or a failure to react in time to a delay. In addition, it puts that information within reach of those who need it, without complicated interfaces.

 

The project benefits:

 

· Mission planners, who can compare sites and dates quickly, anticipate a lack of light or communication, and adjust the plan in time when the mission is delayed.

· Science and engineering teams, who share the same view of the site to coordinate their decisions.

· Educators, who have a visual tool to teach how a real Moon landing is planned.

· The public, who can explore the lunar south pole and understand why light and communication define where and when to land.

 

WHAT TOOLS, PROGRAMMING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, OR SOFTWARE WERE USED?

 
Repository: https://github.com/K4zzu/MoonSite

Front End

· JavaScript with React 19 and Vite 8.

· Three.js (WebGL) for the 3D scene: Earth, Moon, LOLA terrain, multistage rocket, lunar lander, and exhaust and dust particles.

· Web Audio API for synthesized sound, with no audio files.

· SVG graphics for the sky and horizon; printable PDF report and CSV export.

· Bilingual interface (English and Spanish), guided tutorial, keyboard shortcuts, reduced-motion option, and mobile-responsive design.

· Quality: automated tests with the Node.js test runner and static analysis with oxlint. Deployment on AWS Amplify Hosting.

 

Back End

· No server in production: all calculations are done in the browser from static files.

· Data pipeline in Python 3 (NumPy and Pillow): JPL Horizons API queries, reading of the LOLA elevation model, computation of horizons and terrain meshes, textures, and a validation script.

· Hardware: a personal computer; the application runs in any modern desktop or mobile browser.

 

AI

· Logo created with Gemini.

 

HOW IS THE PROJECT CREATIVE?

· Three scales in a single continuous scene: from the Earth–Moon journey to the lunar globe to standing at the site, without switching tools.

· An answer in one color and one sentence: the verdict condenses hours of data into something anyone understands instantly.

· Visible replanning: the encounter point with the Moon slides along the orbit, the previous route remains as a ghost, and the alternatives appear numbered over the scene.

· Cinematic narrative with real physics: a descent profile like that of real missions, a ground camera that follows the landing, and dust that flies out in straight lines because there is no air.

· A real case within the simulation: the IM-2 mission as a ghost route, to understand with a real-world example why the light margin matters.

· A storyline in plain words that explains what is happening at every moment, designed for planners and for the public.

 

WHAT FACTORS DID YOUR TEAM CONSIDER?

· Grazing illumination: at the south pole the Sun never rises more than about 1.5° above the horizon, so any hill can block it for days. That is why we use the real LOLA horizon out to 150 km, seen from 2 m above the ground.

· No atmosphere: the horizon is purely geometric, with no refraction, and the partial solar disk is modeled (±0.27°).

· Direct communication: the visibility of Earth, which at the south pole rises and falls with libration, defines the link windows.

· Verifiable accuracy: we compared against independent Horizons queries (error under 0.005°) and against published studies of polar illumination.

· Landable sites: candidates are located on ridges or, when there is no clear ridge (Haworth and Malapert), at the point with the most sunlight in 2027 with a slope under 8° within 10 km.

· Schedule changes: launch delays are common, so replanning is immediate and shows what improves and what gets worse.

· Accessibility: plain language, two languages, tutorial, mobile use, and a reduced-motion option.

· Known limitations: 120 m terrain resolution, a smooth horizon for sites north of 75° S, and a two-body transfer model for the trajectory.
